lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: name: comprehende

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: description: Groups a git diff into review concerns and opens a local UI so humans can comprehend AI-generated code changes. Use when reviewing a PR, a branch diff, a turn diff, or when the user asks to run comprehende or to upload the report.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: license: MIT

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: compatibility: Requires Node.js 24+, git, and a git work tree as the current working directory.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: # Comprehende

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Group a git diff into review concerns and serve a local UI. The point is cognitive offloading over cognitive surrender: the human gets a why and a what of their own to hold against the live diff, instead of adopting the change blind.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Run every command inside the repository under review. Cwd is the repo; there is no `--repo` flag. Use the pinned CLI:

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ```sh

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: npx comprehende@0.9.1 <command>

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: The review document is interpretation only. It holds a title, groups, summaries, and hunk pointers. Do not copy patch text into it. `serve` reads the diff from git.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Work from the digest, not the diff. The digest is one line per file: kind, hunks, symbols, pairing and copy hints. Grouping needs that line; only ambiguity needs patch text. Fetch patch with `show`, at most 8 fetches per review.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ## Workflow

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Each step is one tool call where the step says so. Batch the commands as written; every extra round trip re-sends the whole context. Spend one tool call per phase: the step-2 batch, one sources call, one show batch, one write, validate. Further calls only fix what validate names.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: 1. Name base and head. Use the refs the user named; three-dot (`base...head`) is the merge request or branch diff. When the change is already on the default branch, use the request's recorded base and head SHAs; the moving default-branch `HEAD` includes later merges. When only the head SHA is known, base is the merge-base of that head with the named base branch. Fetch a ref that is missing from the local clone. Done when both ref names are chosen. The next shell call verifies them.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: 2. One shell call: verify the refs, write the draft, print the digest and the draft, log, and stat. `$REVIEW_DIR` comes from `mktemp -d` in that call (outside the repository; the work tree stays untouched, with no new gitignore entries). `&&` stops the shell before `pregroup` when a ref does not resolve. Stop and tell the user which ref failed, rather than guess a ref.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: ```sh

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: REVIEW_DIR=$(mktemp -d) && git rev-parse --verify --end-of-options "<base>^{commit}" && git rev-parse --verify --end-of-options "<head>^{commit}" && {

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: npm view comprehende version || true

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: npx comprehende@0.9.1 pregroup --base <base> --head <head> --data "$REVIEW_DIR/review.json"

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: npx comprehende@0.9.1 digest --base <base> --head <head>

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: cat "$REVIEW_DIR/review.json"

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: git log --format='%s' --end-of-options <base>...<head>

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: git diff --stat <base>...<head>

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: When the user names a local executable, use that command as written in place of `npx comprehende@0.9.1`, and run `<executable> --version` in this same shell call in place of `npm view`. That printed line is the CLI version.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: If that version is newer than this pin (`npx comprehende@0.9.1`), stop and tell the user. Show `npx skills update` as an option they can run. Do not run that command. Wait for them to continue with this pin, or to update and start this skill again. If the versions match or the query fails, continue. Defaults: `--head` is `HEAD`; `--base` is `origin/HEAD`, falling back to `main` or `master`. `pregroup` writes a draft: identical-copy clusters, one `mechanical` group (renames, copies, moves, generated output), and one `change` group for the rest, with stub prose. It does not invent a review. Done when that file exists and the digest and draft are in context. Trust the `identical copy` and `pairs with` hints; never fetch patch to confirm them. Never read the draft from disk; the `cat` above already printed it.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: 3. One tool call for all sources, truncated at fetch time. Files on disk go through one shell call that caps each file, never a read per file:

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: ```sh

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: for f in "<sourcesDir>"/*; do echo "=== $f"; head -n 40 "$f"; done

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Sources behind a host CLI or MCP go in one parallel block, one fetch each: PR or ticket body to 15 lines, each comment to 10 lines plus its pin, commit log subjects only. Never run a full `git diff`; the digest line is the file. Full bodies stay out of context; the caps above are the source. Done when the digest, the draft, and those sources are in context.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: 4. Recover the why, write the title, write the what, and check each source item against the digest and the fetched hunks (see lookFor). Then write document `title` (always), document `summary` (always), document `why` (only when a source names the motive), and document `lookFor` (only when an item diverges; see lookFor). Summaries come from the digest symbols and kinds, plus fetched hunks where fetched. Replace the stub title and summary. Done when every source item has a verdict, every divergence is a document `lookFor` bullet, every ticket item a later comment changes is a bullet, and every lookFor bullet matches the code at head.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: 5. Group the hunks by review concern, starting from the draft. Accept a draft group that already holds one concern. Split the `change` group where a reader would stop and review the first piece alone. Merge draft groups that serve one concern. A path covers every hunk of its file: keep the draft's path refs, and write hunk refs only for a file split across groups. Fetch patch only to decide a split: state the decision first ("`login.ts` hunks may belong apart"), then batch every fetch in the one show call below. Fetch at most one hunk per 3 files in the digest (at least 2, at most 8). Draft `mirrors`, `mechanical`, and one-concern groups need no fetch:

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ```sh

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: npx comprehende@0.9.1 show --hunk "<ref>"; npx comprehende@0.9.1 show --file "<path>"

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Copy each ref from the draft into the group that holds it, verbatim; the draft refs already match live git. When one file's hunks belong in different groups, name each hunk as in the hunk identity paragraph. Set document `size` from review burden, not `git diff --stat`. Write the whole `review.json` in one write from the field shape below. Keep `version` and `source` from the draft. Done when every ref from the draft is in at least one group, every live hunk of a split file is named, every group has its `why`, stub prose is gone, and every named `part` has a matching document `parts[]` entry. Also done when each unit test sits in the group of the code it checks, each new harness sits with the build or CI that runs it, each feature spec sits with its seed and helpers, each one-line call site or declaration sits with the code it serves, unasked work that could have been its own PR has its own `part`, related enabling work stays one part, each `dependsOn` id names a group in the same `part`, and each mechanical summary says what the reader can skip. When a story builds on another part, `suggestedOrder` puts that part first.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Field shape. The words are placeholders. This shape is enough to write a valid document.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ```json

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "version": 1,

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "source": { "baseRef": "<base>", "headRef": "<head>", "range": "<base>...<head>" },

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "size": "small",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "title": "Short name",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "summary": "What the change is.",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "groups": [

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "id": "helper",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "title": "Group title",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "why": "Why this group exists.",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "summary": "What this group is.",

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "suggestedOrder": 0,

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: "hunkRefs": ["src/file.ts"]

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Add a field when the section that defines it says to write it: document `why`, `lookFor`, and `parts` (`name`, `summary`); `sources` (`id`, `kind` of `ticket`, `pr`, `pr-comment`, `commit`, or `transcript`, `label`, plus `url`, `title`, `gist`, and `part` when you have them). On a group: `part`, `sources` (those ids), `lookFor`, `dependsOn` (group ids). A `pr-comment` source also has `author` and `body`. A line pin adds `path`, `side` (`old` or `new`), and `line` together. `size` is `trivial`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, or `very-large`.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: 6. Run `npx comprehende@0.9.1 validate --data "$REVIEW_DIR/review.json"` with the absolute path. It checks exactly these: every live hunk sits in a group, every ref matches live git, every `source:` id exists in `sources`, every group `part` has a `parts[]` entry, every PR comment pin (`path`, `side`, `line`) matches a live line, and the document has no unknown fields. On failure, fix what the message names; the diff is git's, leave it alone. Done when validate exits 0.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: 7. When they ask to upload the report, follow Export. Otherwise run `npx comprehende@0.9.1 serve --data "$REVIEW_DIR/review.json" --open` and give the user the localhost URL (`127.0.0.1` only).

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: `references/example.md` is an optional filled sample of the field shape. The shape in step 5 is enough to write a document.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ## Export

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Write a static site and put that folder where they asked.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ```sh

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: npx comprehende@0.9.1 export --data "$REVIEW_DIR/review.json" --out "$EXPORT_DIR"

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: `$EXPORT_DIR` is a fresh directory outside the work tree, not a git repository. The folder is the UI plus frozen git payloads. There is no git in it. Done when they have the URL or path they named. If `review.json` is still a draft, finish the Workflow through validate, then export.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ## The title

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Document `title` is a short name for the whole change. Always write one.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Prefer a title the human already wrote when it names this change: the pull request title, a ticket title, or the name they used in a transcript. Keep that wording when it is descriptive and represents the reviewed change.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Invent a title when those sources are missing, vague, or name something else. A branch slug, "WIP", or "fix" is not a title. Sources are a reference. Do not paste a title that does not fit.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ## The why

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Document `why` names why the work exists, in one or two sentences, inferred only from the sources below. It is the problem or goal a source states. Before writing it, find the source sentence that states that problem or goal: "Support SSO login", "so admins can export audit logs", "retries flood the API". A sentence that only says what the change does ("the settings page becomes a modal", "uploads move to S3") belongs in the summary. When no source sentence states a problem or goal, or the sources are mixed, omit the why. Write it in the source's own terms, with no cause, benefit, or reader need the source does not name. The same holds for every group `why`: a citation carries only what that source says, and a source is the reason for a choice only when it states that reason. Do not derive document `why` from the digest, from group structure, or from a motive you infer from the patch. A request naming two unrelated product stories with no unifying source also gets no document `why`; each story keeps its own group `why`s.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Sources are read truncated, never copied into the review document, except PR review comments: copy `author` and `body` so the UI can show the quote. Keep ticket bodies, request descriptions, commit text, and transcript text out of `review.json`. Cite a source in prose with `[text](source:s1)` when that sentence leans on it.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - Tickets and issues. Emit a `sources` item: short `id` (`s1`), `kind` `ticket`, `label` (`#24`), plus `url`, `title`, `gist`, and `part` when you have them. Read the ticket (host CLI, tools or MCP, whichever is available) when document `why` needs it. `part` goes on a ticket that belongs to one story, matching that story's group `part`; omit it only when the request or ticket title says the ticket covers the whole review. Commit count proves nothing about ticket scope. Do not copy the ticket body.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - Pull request. When the user named a pull request or merge request, emit `kind` `pr` with a label like `PR #32` and a gist from the description. Do not copy the description. PRs can also refer to tickets and issues in their description or branch names.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - PR comments. Emit `kind` `pr-comment`. Label like `alice on PR #32`. Copy `author` and `body`. For a review comment on a line, also copy `path`, `side` (`old` or `new`, git-shaped, not GitHub LEFT/RIGHT), and `line`. A conversation comment has no pin. Flatten threads: one source per comment.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - Commit messages. `git log --format='%s' --end-of-options <base>...<head>`. Emit `kind` `commit` when a commit names the motive. `label` is that subject line, or a SHA from the same log. They can clarify group `why`; document `why` needs one of the stronger sources above. These can also contain issues and tickets.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - Transcripts. A coding-agent (like Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, etc.) transcript you already have (this session, or a historical one) supplies the human's stated reason. Emit `kind` `transcript`, a label like `Cursor session · Aug 12`, and a gist. Omit `url`. Do not copy transcript text.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Put those ids on the group `sources` array when the group uses them, even if the prose does not cite them inline. `validate` fails on a `source:` href whose id is missing from `sources`.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Every group has `why`: why this group exists. A source that names the concern is best. A foundation group with no source of its own says it enables the groups that depend on it; that is a complete `why`. Independent side work in its own part (docs-only, test-only) gets its own group `why` and leaves document `why` to the named motive.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ## The what

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Document `summary` is one or two sentences naming what the change is, including each independent story when the PR is mixed. Every review has one, even when `why` is absent. It is a what, not a motive.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: When groups use `part`, write one document `parts[]` entry per independent story. `name` is that `part` string. `summary` is one sentence saying what that story is, same voice as group `summary`. Document `summary` still names the stories; the part summary is the per-story what under the colored Overview column. Omit `parts` when no group has `part`.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Group `summary` is one sentence saying what the group is, describing how its hunks are related: "Calling the new validator from `core.ts` by the route in `routes.ts`", not a file-by-file recap or a path list. For draft `mirrors` and `mechanical` groups kept as-is, the summary says what the reader can skip and why that is safe: an identical copy, a pure move, or regenerated output that means the same.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ## Grouping rules

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - Group by review concern: why these hunks are read together. A directory qualifies only when that directory is the concern. The digest line plus the draft is enough for most files; the patch is for ambiguity only.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - A group is one concern a reviewer names in a phrase. The code, the unit tests that check it, and the one-line call sites, declarations, and re-exports that serve it read together in that group. A unit test next to its module stays in that module's group; the digest `pairs with` hint names that module. A new integration harness is the concern: that harness and the build or CI files that run it are one group, not the production group they exercise. A new feature's code, fixtures, seeds, helpers, and the spec that runs them are one group. A seed or helper that only one spec uses stays in that spec's group. A foundation split is for a contract several later groups share. Split a concern only where a reader would stop and review the first piece alone. A small change has one to three groups.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - A hunk may appear in several groups when it matters in more than one story. When one hunk holds two concerns, the group that holds it names both.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - `dependsOn` marks a real dependency inside one story: the reader needs the earlier group to understand this one. It stays inside one part. Reading order inside a story: contracts and foundations, then call sites, then mechanical work. Independent work stands alone with its own `part`, empty `dependsOn`, and nothing depending on it. A second feature, extra product events, a dependency policy change, or standalone documentation that could have been its own PR is independent work. Unasked work that only enables the asked story (path renames, fixture layout, local startup) stays one part with that story, or one harness part. When unsure whether two concerns depend on each other, keep them separate under different parts: a false split is easy to see, a false chain hides a mixed PR.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - `part` is a short name (a few words) for one independent story, the same on every group in that story; the UI colors shared parts together. One document `parts[]` entry per name.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - Mechanical work (import reordering, identifier-only renames, generated code, formatting, pure moves) is its own group that keeps every hunk as refs, risk visible rather than folded into a file list. The draft `mechanical` group already holds the CLI-flagged files; check each line still belongs (a flagged file with a real behavior change moves out to its story) and write the summary that says what the reader can skip. An identical copy of a file in the draft `mirrors` group sits with its source; that group's summary still says the copy is identical. When a mechanical group exists only because of a story, it is that part's last group with nothing depending on it. When it could have been its own PR, it is its own part.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - `suggestedOrder` walks the whole review, independent parts included. Mechanical parts, independent documentation, and test-only cleanup go last.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - Document `size` is human review burden: `trivial`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `very-large`. Forty files changing one import in one group are `small`. A new component plus follow-up changes across existing screens is `medium`. A new contract that later groups depend on is `large`. That `size` stays when those groups merge. The digest header (file and hunk counts) sets the starting point; the group count and dependencies adjust it.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - Coverage: every live hunk sits in at least one group. A path covers every live hunk of that file. Duplicate refs across groups are allowed. Unreferenced hunks fail `validate` and show as Unassigned in the UI. Every ref in the draft already covers its hunks; splitting a file across groups needs hunk refs, everything else keeps the draft's paths.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - Lockfiles have no hunk refs; the CLI leaves them out of the draft and the UI gives them their own closed bucket. Hunk refs exist only for hunks the draft lists.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: - A path stays valid when a rebase only shifts line numbers. `path@oldStart+newStart` goes stale when those starts move, and that fails `validate`. `serve` still starts, shows git at those SHAs, and flags the broken pointer. Re-run `pregroup` and copy fresh refs. A dirty work tree does not make refs stale.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: A `hunkRefs` entry is a path string when the group holds every live hunk of that file. Copy the path from the draft. When a file is split across groups, name each hunk as `path@oldStart+newStart`, or `old/path -> new/path@oldStart+newStart` when that hunk is a rename. Take `oldStart` and `newStart` from the digest `show` of that file, or from the hunk's `@@ -oldStart,oldLines +newStart,newLines @@` header. Identity is `(path, oldStart, newStart)` plus `oldPath` when renamed. Image files are paths. Git LFS images are read from `.git/lfs/objects` in the clone; a missing object leaves the image slot empty.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ## lookFor

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: `lookFor` is for what a careful engineer would miss on a first read of the live diff. Default to an empty `lookFor` and earn each bullet with a fetch: a bullet lives only where you ran `show` on its hunks, or where the digest plus the sources already prove it. Each bullet is one finding, stated as fact and true at head: optionally a short risk tag (Subtle, Breaking, Race, Perf), then one sentence on what the code at head does and what the reader would observe. The human checks it against the live diff and keeps the verdict. Pseudocode, diagrams, collapsed diffs, commit lists, hunk counts, and pass/fail marks stay out.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Group `lookFor` holds claims that live in those hunks. Fetch the hunk when a behavior change hides in it and write the predicted trace: a small realistic input, where the old and new paths diverge, and the observable result. A change in equality or identity (object versus primitive fields, pointer versus contents) uses two inputs that look the same and now compare differently. When a hunk works around app behavior (a sleep, a forced write, a retry), the bullet says what the app does without the workaround. A hunk under application source in a PR whose sources are about tests, CI, or tooling is production code in a test PR: the bullet says it is production code and names that behavior change. A setup or teardown script that deletes or overwrites a file that is not test output earns a bullet: the path, when it happens, and what the developer loses. So does a behavior change no source mentions, and a hunk that resolves a review comment in a way the hunk alone does not make obvious: the bullet says what the fix does. Empty is correct for a rename, a formatting change, or a wording-only docs group; leave it empty rather than fill it. Draft `mirrors` and `mechanical` groups stay empty unless a fetch proves otherwise.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.text: Document `lookFor` holds claims about the whole change, and the divergences between the sources and the code at head. Source items are each requirement and acceptance item in a ticket, each behavior claim in the pull request description and commit messages, and each request in a review comment. Test plans, manual QA notes, and out-of-scope lists are context, not items. Read the truncated source for each item and give it a verdict: done as asked, done differently, not done, or not true at head. Each verdict other than done-as-asked is one bullet: what the source asks or says, what the digest or fetched hunk shows, and the reason when a source or the code gives one, or that no source gives one. When a later source changes what an earlier one asked (a review comment overrides the ticket), the ticket item is done differently, and the bullet names both sources. A manual step a source says the change needs (turn on a setting, run a migration) is also a bullet. Cite with `[text](source:s1)`; the id goes in `sources`, and `validate` fails on an unknown id. Omit the field when nothing needs a bullet.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: ## Write the prose

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: Document `title`, document `why`, group `why`, `summary`, and `lookFor` are for a tired engineer on the first read.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - One thought per sentence; split past about 25 words.

lines.author: Cursor Agent
lines.text: - Present tense. Name who does what.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - Use the real symbol, path, flag, or command.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - Cut every word that does no work. No changelog voice, no puffery, no "not just X, but Y".

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - A straightforward group needs only its title, `why`, and `summary`; the live diff does the rest.
